plot: Odo and Mothwick follow the true story of the Cottingley Fairies (1917): two cousins photograph fairies by the beck, experts and Arthur Conan Doyle believe them, and in 1983 they confess the fairies were paper cut from a book — except Frances swears the fifth photo was real, and something small watches Odo's lantern by the water.

beats.say: Elsie, quick! They're dancing right in front of me! Take it!
A true story. Cottingley, England, nineteen seventeen. Two girls and a camera.
Their photos fooled the world. So what did these girls really see?
New episode every day — subscribe so you don't miss what happens next.
Small footprints in a sealed tomb... and now fairies?
Those footprints ran north, Odo. Into these very woods.
Elsie Wright was sixteen. Her cousin, Frances Griffiths, was nine.
Frances had come from South Africa. She brought a picture book.
She kept coming home soaked from the beck, the stream nearby.
I only go down there to see the fairies. That's all.
Lend us your camera, Father. We'll prove it to you.
Her father lent them his camera. They ran straight to the stream.
In his darkroom, a picture appeared. Frances, and tiny dancing fairies.
Cardboard cutouts, that's all. A prank, girls. Nothing more.
Then came a gnome. After that, he stopped lending them his camera.
Why would two young girls lie about fairies?
Who said they lied? Wait until you hear who believed them.
In nineteen nineteen, Elsie's mother took the photos to a Bradford meeting.
A photography expert, Harold Snelling, studied the glass negatives.
He found no sign of cutouts, and no studio tricks.
Kodak found no faking either, but refused to certify them.
In summer nineteen twenty, the girls got new cameras and marked plates.
Three more photos. A leaping fairy, flowers offered, a sunbath.
Then came the most famous believer of all. Arthur Conan Doyle.
Fairies, photographed at last! The whole world must see this.
The creator of Sherlock Holmes wrote about them in December nineteen twenty.
The magazine sold out within days.
If Sherlock Holmes's creator believed them, who would dare doubt?
In nineteen sixty-six, a reporter found Elsie and asked her again.
Perhaps I photographed my own thoughts. Who can say?
Ten years later, both women were asked on television. Both denied faking.
Sixty years of questions, Odo. And they still would not say fake.
Then, in nineteen eighty-three, they finally confessed. The fairies were paper.
Elsie had copied them from that picture book Frances brought.
Hatpins held them up. Afterwards, we threw them in the beck.
So it was all a trick. Every single photo.
Not every one, Odo. Not according to Frances.
Elsie said the fifth photo was faked like all the others.
No. That last one is real. I know what I saw.
Both women still said that they really had seen fairies.
And each of them claimed that she had taken the fifth photo.
Two cousins, one photo, and two different stories.
More than a hundred years later, that fifth photograph still divides people.
Odo... by the water. Something small just looked at your lantern.
Next time: hundreds of witnesses, one harbour, and a sea serpent.
What do you think happens in the next part? Tell me in the comments.

long.description:
What do you think happens in the next part? Tell me in the comments.

"They admitted the trick. So why did one of them swear the last photo was real?" — Odo

A true story from Cottingley, England: in 1917 two cousins photographed fairies by a stream, and experts and Arthur Conan Doyle believed them. In 1983 they confessed — but Frances never gave up the fifth photograph.
